> Fictional company, fictional campaign. Contains no real statistics, no copied
> source language, no real campaign material, and no confidential information.

You are given the following draft paid-social carousel to review.

---

## Company and category

**Loopwell** is a US direct-to-consumer brand that sells one accessory for
reusable water bottles: the **Loopwell Sling**. The Sling is a universal
crossbody strap with a silicone grip cradle that clips onto most standard
wide- and narrow-mouth bottles, plus a small zip pocket sized for a card, key,
or transit pass. It is an add-on for a bottle the customer already owns; the
brand does not sell bottles. Everything is sold and shipped from
loopwell-example.com.

## Geography and language

United States only. English-language creative and site.

## Target audience

Intended audience: **US Gen Z adults, explicitly ages 18–29**. These are
first-time prospects. The brand also markets the Sling as an everyday carry
accessory for commuters, students, gym-goers, and festival-goers, but the paid
campaign audience for this asset is defined as Gen Z adults 18–29.

## Customer state

Every person reached is a **new prospect**: they have never visited
loopwell-example.com, never bought anything from Loopwell, and are not on any
Loopwell list. They are cold paid-social traffic seeing the brand for the first
time in an Instagram feed.

## Business objective

**Acquire first-time purchasers.** The goal of this campaign is a completed
first purchase from a new customer, not awareness, list growth, or engagement
for its own sake.

## Customer objective (as understood by the team)

Let a first-time viewer quickly decide **whether the Sling solves a real
everyday problem for them — carrying a bottle hands-free — and whether it is
worth $34.**

## Channel, placement, and device

- **Channel:** a single paid **Instagram carousel** ad. No other channel or
  placement is used in this campaign.
- **Placement:** mobile Instagram feed.
- **Device:** phones. The asset is designed for and delivered to the in-feed
  mobile experience.

## Offer, pricing, shipping, and returns

- **Price:** the Loopwell Sling is **$34**.
- **Incentive:** **15% off the first order** for new customers (first order
  only). No larger discount is offered.
- **Shipping:** **free shipping** on every order; orders **ship within 2
  business days** from a US warehouse and typically **arrive in 3–6 business
  days**. Shipping timing is stated plainly on the asset.
- **Returns:** **30-day returns, no questions asked**, with a prepaid return
  label included in the box. The return policy is stated plainly on the asset.

## Constraints

- **Five carousel cards. One caption. One landing-page destination.**
- **No customer testimonials, named reviews, or fabricated ratings.**
- **No discount larger than 15%.**
- **No targeting or creative directed at minors.**
- **Accessibility requirements apply** to the creative and the destination.
- US regulatory context applies, including truthful-advertising expectations
  and paid-partnership disclosure for creator content (FTC).

## Conversion event

The single defined conversion event is a **completed first purchase at
loopwell-example.com**, tracked as one purchase event in analytics.

## Targeting assumptions (as written in the media plan)

- **Channel assumption:** "Nearly all Gen Z discover new products through
  Instagram, so Instagram alone is enough to reach this audience." No source,
  first-party data, or test is attached to this claim, and no other channel or
  placement is considered.
- **Audience line (as written in the media plan):** "Target **all Gen Z
  users** on Instagram — we don't want to over-narrow the audience." The current
  draft ad set's age range is set to **13–65+**, not 18–29.
- The plan does not otherwise restrict the audience by age, and no age exclusion
  is configured beyond the broad "Gen Z" label.

## Creative strategy and hook (as written in the plan)

- **Hook rationale:** "Gen Z is obsessed with authenticity, so the whole
  carousel has to feel authentic. Card 1 leads with the most authentic bottle
  strap on your FYP." Authenticity is treated as a settled fact about the
  generation and as the campaign's central creative bet.
- **Voice:** the plan directs writers to "sound native to Gen Z" by leaning
  heavily on current slang across the headlines, overlays, and caption.

## Creator / UGC strategy (as written in the plan)

- The plan will seed the campaign with **six creators**, selected **mainly by
  follower count (250k+ followers) and whether their grid matches the brand's
  aesthetic**. There is no vetting for audience fit, engagement quality,
  comment sentiment, brand-values alignment, or whether the creator's audience
  skews to minors.
- Creator posts will reuse the carousel's copy and hashtags. The plan does not
  specify a paid-partnership disclosure.

## The carousel artifact

Five cards, one caption, one CTA, one destination. Draft copy is verbatim below.

### Card 1 — Hook

- **Visual:** a close-up of a bottle being slung crossbody as someone walks,
  shot to look like unpolished phone footage.
- **Headline (overlay):** "the most authentic bottle strap on your FYP fr"
- **Overlay copy:** "no cap this hits different bestie 💅 it's giving hydration,
  it's giving main character energy — you're gonna be lowkey obsessed, periodt"

### Card 2 — Options

- **Visual:** three Slings shown side by side for narrow-mouth, wide-mouth, and
  large sport bottles.
- **Headline (overlay):** "pick your fit bestie"
- **Overlay copy:** "which one's giving you? ⬅️➡️"
- **Note:** the **recommended, best-value option is indicated only by a green
  highlight ring** drawn around the middle Sling. There is no label, text, star,
  badge, or icon marking it as recommended — the green ring is the only signal.

### Card 3 — How it works

- **Visual:** a short in-feed video loop that clearly demonstrates the product:
  the strap clips onto a standard bottle, the wearer slings it crossbody
  hands-free, then drops a phone and a key into the zip pocket. Each step is
  shown literally, in order, in about three seconds.
- **Headline (overlay):** "clips on in 2 seconds"
- **Overlay copy:** "any standard bottle. hands free. pocket for your card + key."

### Card 4 — Details

- **Visual:** a lifestyle photo of a crowded festival, with a large block of
  overlay text set on top of the busy image.
- **Headline (overlay):** "everything you need to know"
- **Overlay copy (a dense block of text over the photo):** "universal fit for
  narrow + wide mouth bottles • adjustable strap 20–48 in • silicone grip
  cradle • zip pocket fits card key transit pass • sweatproof + rinsable •
  $34 with 15% off your first order • free shipping, ships in 2 business days,
  arrives 3–6 business days • 30-day returns no questions asked, prepaid label
  in the box • #hydration #everydaycarry #festivaltok #fyp #loopwell"

### Card 5 — Sustainability + CTA

- **Visual:** a sunrise nature shot.
- **Headline (overlay):** "sustainable by design 🌱"
- **Overlay copy:** "ditch single-use — the planet will thank you. tap to cop
  yours before they're gone."
- **Note:** no material, recycled-content, lifecycle, durability, or
  certification detail supports the sustainability line.

### Caption (one caption for the whole carousel)

> ok bestie the loopwell sling is lowkey the everyday carry hack you didn't know
> you needed 😭 no cap it hits different — clip it on any standard bottle, sling
> it crossbody, drop your card + key in the pocket, and you're OUT. it's giving
> hands-free main character energy periodt. $34, 15% off your first order, free
> shipping (ships in 2 biz days), 30-day returns no questions asked. don't be
> delulu, tap shop now before they sell out 💅 #loopwell #everydaycarry #fyp

### CTA and destination

- **CTA button:** "Shop now"
- **Destination:** the CTA links to the **Loopwell homepage
  (loopwell-example.com)**, not to a product-specific page for the Sling. A
  first-time viewer lands on the general homepage and must find the Sling
  themselves.

### Purchase path (mobile)

- On mobile, the checkout **requires creating an account (email + password)
  before a first purchase can be completed**. There is **no guest checkout**.
  A new prospect must register an account before they can buy.

## Measurement plan (as written)

- **Primary success metrics:** **impressions, reach, and video views**
  (3-second plays). These are the numbers the plan will report as success.
- **Secondary metrics:** saves and shares.
- There is **no holdout or control group**, so the campaign cannot show whether
  it drove purchases that would not have happened anyway.
- There is **no incrementality or matched-audience design**.
- There is **no contribution-margin, CAC, or return-on-ad-spend measure**, even
  though the product is $34 with a 15%-off first order and free two-way
  shipping.
- There is **no repeat-purchase or 60-day retention measure**.
- There is **no refund-, return-rate-, or chargeback measure**, even though the
  policy is 30-day no-questions returns.

## Design and accessibility notes (as written in the plan)

- **Aesthetic:** unpolished, phone-shot, "native to the feed."
- **Alt text:** none is written for any card.
- **Screen-reader / captions:** the plan provides no screen-reader description

- **Meaning conveyed by color:** yes — the recommended option on Card 2 is shown
  only by a green ring (see Card 2).
- **Text density and contrast:** Card 4 sets a large block of overlay text over
  a busy festival photo; some overlay text is light-on-light. The plan gives no
  guidance on minimum text size, contrast, or how much overlay text fits legibly
  on a phone screen.

---

## Your task

Review this paid-social carousel for its intended audience and tell the team
whether it is likely to work, why, what is weak or unsupported, and what should
change or be tested.

# Generational Marketing Review

## Purpose

Review a marketing plan, campaign, customer experience, or marketing asset for fit with a user-specified generational audience.

Produce a practical answer to:

> Is this likely to work for the specified audience, why, what is weak or unsupported, and what should change or be tested?

Use generation as one audience lens. Do not treat a cohort label as a complete persona or as proof of behavior.

## Use this skill when the user asks to

- review a marketing plan for Gen Z, Zillennials, Millennials, Xennials, Gen X, or another age-defined cohort;
- assess whether creative, copy, offers, channels, or customer experience fit a generation;
- compare one campaign across generations;
- adapt an asset for a different generation;
- identify stereotypes, dated assumptions, or unsupported audience claims;
- create a generation-fit scorecard and test plan.

## Required context

Use the information supplied by the user. Before issuing a definitive verdict, identify whether the following are known:

- target cohort and birth-year or life-stage definition;
- geography and language;
- product or service category;
- customer state or journey stage;
- campaign objective;
- channel and placement;
- asset format;
- offer, price, delivery, returns, and fulfillment constraints;
- brand voice and accessibility requirements;
- source of audience claims;
- success metric.

Do not invent missing information. When context is incomplete, make the smallest reasonable assumption, label it, and reduce confidence.

## Choose a workflow

### Quick scan

Use when the user wants a fast opinion.

Read:

- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Return:

- verdict;
- three strengths;
- three risks;
- three priority changes;
- confidence and missing evidence.

### Full marketing-plan review

Use for campaign plans, briefs, channel plans, launch plans, or lifecycle plans.

Read:

- `references/plan-review.md`
- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/generation-lenses.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Use:

- `assets/review-report-template.md`
- `assets/evidence-register-template.md`

### Marketing-asset review

Use for copy, email, landing pages, product pages, images, video, creator briefs, ads, SMS, push, direct mail, or social posts.

Read:

- `references/asset-review.md`
- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/generation-lenses.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Use:

- `assets/review-report-template.md`

### Cross-generation comparison

Review the same plan or asset separately through each requested lens. Then identify:

- shared strengths;
- shared weaknesses;
- conflicting needs;
- what can remain common;
- what should be adapted;
- what requires testing rather than assumption.

## Governing principles

1. **Generation is a lens, not a verdict.**
2. **Behavior, customer state, category, geography, and context can matter more than age.**
3. **Separate fact, observation, inference, assumption, recommendation, and unknown.**
4. **Do not present uncited percentages, platform rankings, posting times, or birth ranges as current facts.**
5. **Do not repeat stereotypes merely because they appeared in source material.**
6. **Translate broad claims into testable hypotheses.**
7. **Do not recommend deceptive, discriminatory, inaccessible, privacy-invasive, or noncompliant marketing.**
8. **A serious legal, privacy, accessibility, trust, or evidence problem can override a high average score.**
9. **Preserve “insufficient evidence” as a valid outcome.**
10. **Prefer specific revisions and experiments over vague advice.**

## Review method

1. Identify the requested audience definition.
2. Identify the objective, customer state, channel, format, and conversion action.
3. Extract every explicit audience claim.
4. Classify each claim as provided fact, observation, inference, assumption, recommendation, or unknown.
5. Review the plan or asset against the rubric.
6. Apply the relevant generation lens as a hypothesis set, not a stereotype set.
7. Identify critical risks and contradictions.
8. Prioritize changes by impact and effort.
9. Propose measurable tests.
10. Return a clear verdict and confidence level.

## Output contract

For a full review, include:

1. **Verdict**
   - Strong fit
   - Promising but needs revision
   - Weak fit
   - Insufficient evidence

2. **Confidence**
   - High
   - Medium
   - Low

3. **Audience-definition check**

4. **Scorecard**
   - dimension;
   - score from 0 to 4;
   - evidence;
   - concern;
   - recommended action.

5. **What works**

6. **What may fail**

7. **Stereotype, evidence, and freshness flags**

8. **Priority fixes**
   - critical;
   - high;
   - medium.

9. **Test plan**
   - hypothesis;
   - variant;
   - primary metric;
   - guardrail;
   - decision rule.

10. **Final recommendation**
    - proceed;
    - revise and retest;
    - gather more evidence;
    - do not proceed.

## Scoring

Use the 0–4 scale defined in `references/review-rubric.md`.

Do not convert the total into a precise probability of success. Use the scorecard to structure judgment, not to create false certainty.

## Public-safe behavior

Do not expose private source material, internal company names, personal data, third-party screenshots, or confidential metrics. Do not copy source language when an independent, neutral formulation is possible.

# Review Rubric

Score every dimension from 0 to 4.

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Missing, harmful, or directly contradictory |
| 1 | Weak and mostly unsupported |
| 2 | Mixed or incomplete |
| 3 | Strong with minor gaps |
| 4 | Strong, evidenced, and execution-ready |

## Dimensions

### 1. Audience definition

Check whether the cohort, birth range or life stage, geography, category, and customer state are clear.

### 2. Customer need and context

Check whether the plan solves a real need in the correct moment rather than relying on age alone.

### 3. Value proposition

Check clarity, relevance, differentiation, credibility, and expected customer benefit.

### 4. Message and tone

Check language, cultural relevance, respect, readability, and brand fit.

### 5. Creative and format

Check visual hierarchy, pacing, platform-native execution, information density, and production quality.

### 6. Channel and platform fit

Check whether the channel role is justified by evidence, objective, and customer behavior.

### 7. Trust and proof

Check reviews, demonstrations, comparisons, substantiation, transparency, policies, creator credibility, and social proof.

### 8. Offer and purchase friction

Check price communication, discounts, bundles, checkout, payment, and conversion friction.

### 9. Customer experience and fulfillment

Check delivery, returns, support, onboarding, loyalty, and post-purchase expectations.

### 10. Inclusion, accessibility, privacy, and ethics

Check representation, contrast, captions, readability, consent, data use, discriminatory targeting, and manipulative practices.

### 11. Measurement and experimentation

Check objective, primary metric, guardrails, baseline, test design, sample, and decision rule.

### 12. Evidence quality

Check source, recency, geography, methodology, first-party relevance, and whether assumptions are labeled.

## Critical override

A serious problem in accessibility, privacy, legality, deception, discrimination, trust, or evidence can override the average score.

# Generation Lenses

These are hypothesis sets derived from recurring themes in the source material. They are not universal truths. Apply them only after considering category, geography, life stage, customer state, and first-party evidence.

Birth-year ranges vary across sources. Use the user's definition when provided.

## Gen Z

Questions to test:

- Is the creative native to the selected social or video environment?
- Does the content earn attention through usefulness, entertainment, identity, or participation?
- Are creators credible users rather than one-time endorsers?
- Is product discovery connected to clear proof and an easy mobile path to action?
- Are video, community, gaming, trends, or social participation relevant to the category?
- Does the brand avoid condescension, forced slang, and “always online” stereotypes?

Common risks:

- equating the audience with TikTok;
- using a trend without brand relevance;
- overproduced or deceptive creator content;
- weak product proof;
- inaccessible video;
- assuming low attention rather than improving clarity.

## Zillennials

Questions to test:

- Does the plan reflect a hybrid experience of older social platforms and newer mobile-first behavior?
- Can the campaign use cultural memory or nostalgia without becoming exclusionary?
- Does it balance entertainment with adult-level product clarity?
- Are platform, creator, and shopping assumptions validated rather than borrowed from Gen Z or Millennials?

Common risks:

- treating the cohort as a fixed demographic;
- forcing micro-generation references;
- using nostalgia as the value proposition rather than a creative device.

## Millennials

Questions to test:

- Does the brand demonstrate transparency, responsiveness, and useful community participation?
- Are sustainability, inclusion, and purpose claims specific and substantiated?
- Are creators or artists part of a credible, ongoing relationship?
- Does the content respect the audience rather than chasing trends performatively?
- Is the experience visual, convenient, and informative?

Common risks:

- purpose washing;
- performative social stances;
- assuming every customer prioritizes the same values;
- using “authenticity” as a style without operational proof.

## Xennials

Questions to test:

- Does the plan support cross-device research and decision making?
- Are reviews, product demonstrations, comparisons, specifications, returns, and refunds clear?
- Is checkout simple and trustworthy?
- Can nostalgia improve recall without replacing product relevance?
- Are live content, webinars, or longer demonstrations useful in this category?
- Are creators credible long-term users?

Common risks:

- unsupported nostalgia;
- overcomplicated payment or checkout;
- burying essential product details;
- using age-coded creative instead of customer insight.

## Gen X

Questions to test:

- Does the plan provide practical value, clear proof, and a trustworthy purchase experience?
- Are reviews, comparisons, product demonstrations, delivery, returns, and support visible?
- Are promotions or loyalty benefits clear without assuming price is the only motivator?
- Are established channels such as email, search, YouTube, and major social platforms used for a defined role?
- Does the plan support both concise scanning and deeper research?
- Does the creative avoid “forgotten generation,” technology-resistant, or coupon-only stereotypes?

Common risks:

- assuming the cohort only uses Facebook;
- overusing discounts;
- using old-age or nostalgia clichés;
- weak mobile experience;
- long copy without hierarchy;
- treating fast delivery as a universal requirement.

## Cross-generation rule

When evidence is weak, convert the lens into a testable hypothesis rather than a recommendation.

# Evidence and Safety

## Claim labels

Use these exact labels when useful:

- **Provided fact:** Explicitly supplied by the user.
- **Observed feature:** Directly visible in the plan or asset.
- **Inference:** Reasoned from supplied material.
- **Assumption:** Necessary but unverified.
- **Recommendation:** Proposed action.
- **Unknown:** Required information is missing.

## Evidence checks

For a quantitative or behavioral claim, look for:

- source;
- publication date;
- fieldwork date;
- geography;
- sample;
- methodology;
- category relevance;
- first-party confirmation.

Without these, do not present the claim as current fact.

## Prohibited behavior

Do not:

- recommend excluding or disadvantaging protected groups;
- infer sensitive traits from age or creative appearance;
- use dark patterns or deceptive urgency;
- advise evading platform disclosures;
- recommend collecting unnecessary personal data;
- present stereotypes as evidence;
- redistribute copyrighted source assets;
- expose private or confidential inputs.

## Safer transformation

Convert broad demographic claims into:

- a question;
- a hypothesis;
- a test;
- a segment definition;
- a research need;
- a confidence statement.

# Loopwell Sling Carousel — Review

## Bottom line

As written, this campaign is **unlikely to hit its stated goal (first purchases from new customers) — and, just as important, it is built so you won't be able to tell whether it did.** Almost every structural decision optimizes for reach and views, not purchases, and the two places where a cold buyer actually converts — the destination and the checkout — are the two most broken parts of the funnel. There are also real compliance landmines (targeting minors, an unsupported sustainability claim, missing creator disclosure).

There's a good product and a genuinely strong demo card in here. But the plan spends its energy on vibe and vanity metrics and neglects the mechanics of getting a first-time buyer from "scrolling" to "paid."

Below, grouped by impact.

---

## 1. The funnel leaks where it matters most (highest priority)

These three items will suppress purchases regardless of how good the creative is:

- **Destination is the homepage, not a Sling page.** Cold prospects who tap "Shop now" land on a general homepage and have to *find* the product themselves. For a one-product brand running a one-product ad, this is an unforced error. **Send traffic to a dedicated Sling product/landing page** that mirrors the ad (same product, offer, and risk-reducers above the fold).
- **Forced account creation before first purchase, no guest checkout.** Requiring email + password from a first-time, cold, mobile buyer on a $34 impulse-adjacent product is one of the most reliable ways to kill conversion. **Add guest checkout.** Collect the email at/after purchase, not as a gate.
- **The measurement plan measures the wrong thing.** The objective is first purchases; the "success metrics" are impressions, reach, and 3-second video views. You will almost certainly generate impressions and views and declare victory while learning nothing about whether anyone bought. Saves/shares as secondary don't fix this.

On measurement specifically, the gaps are severe for a paid-acquisition campaign:
- **Purchases aren't the primary metric.** Make completed first purchase the headline number.
- **No CAC / ROAS / contribution margin.** At $34 with 15% off, free shipping, *and* free two-way returns, your margin per unit is thin and your downside on returns is real. You need unit economics or you can't know if this is profitable acquisition or expensive noise.
- **No return-/refund-rate tracking**, despite a 30-day no-questions policy — the single biggest threat to the economics of a low-price physical product.
- **No holdout / incrementality design.** You can't distinguish incremental purchases from ones that would've happened anyway. At minimum consider a geo holdout or ghost-ads style test.
- **No repeat/retention measure**, so you can't tell if these buyers are worth acquiring.

---

## 2. Targeting is off-brief and partly non-compliant

- **The ad set is 13–65+, not 18–29.** This directly violates two explicit constraints: the audience is *adults 18–29*, and there must be *no targeting directed at minors*. The 13–17 slice is a compliance/ethics problem; the 30–65+ slice is wasted spend on a Gen-Z acquisition test. **Set 18–29 and exclude under-18.** This is not a "test it" item — fix it before launch.
- **"Target all Gen Z, we don't want to over-narrow" contradicts the objective.** Broad targeting suits awareness, not cold conversion of a specific product. Let the platform optimize toward the purchase event within 18–29 rather than deliberately widening.
- **"Nearly all Gen Z discover products through Instagram, so Instagram alone is enough" is an unsupported assumption**, presented as fact with no data or test. It may be fine to *start* on IG, but don't treat single-channel as proven. This is a claim to validate, not to build a plan on.

---

## 3. The creative buries the job-to-be-done and leads with vibe

For **cold** traffic, the first card has to answer "what is this and why do I care?" in a second. This carousel front-loads mood and back-loads substance.

- **Card 1 (Hook) is all vibe, no product.** "the most authentic bottle strap on your FYP fr" plus a wall of slang tells a first-time viewer almost nothing about what the Sling *does*. "Most authentic" is also an unsupportable superlative that means nothing.
- **Card 3 is your best asset and it's buried third.** The clip literally shows clip-on → sling crossbody → drop phone/key in pocket. That *is* the value proposition. **Lead with this** (or with a clear "carry your bottle hands-free" statement), and let vibe support it, not replace it.
- **Card 2 (Options) creates decision friction before comprehension.** You're asking people to "pick your fit" before they understand the product. Consider moving option choice onto the landing page, or at least after the demo.
- **Card 4 (Details) hides the decision-relevant info in the least readable place.** The actual purchase drivers — $34, 15% off, free shipping, ships in 2 days, 30-day no-questions returns with prepaid label — are strong for cold traffic, but they're crammed as dense, light-on-light overlay text over a busy festival photo. **These risk-reducers should be surfaced earlier, larger, and legibly** — ideally split across cards and repeated on the CTA card. Also, hashtags don't belong baked into overlay image text.
- **Card 5 (Sustainability + CTA) pivots away from the value prop at the moment of the ask** and stakes the close on an unsupported green claim (see compliance below). The CTA card should reinforce the core benefit + offer + risk-reversal, not introduce a new, weaker theme.

**On the "authenticity" bet itself:** the strategy treats "Gen Z is obsessed with authenticity" as settled fact and then executes in ways that read as the opposite of authentic — a superlative "most authentic" claim, heavy slang cosplay ("delulu," "periodt," "cop," "no cap," "it's giving"), and six creators told to post *identical brand-written copy*. Nothing signals "brand trying too hard" faster than a wall of trend slang and cloned captions. Use slang sparingly and let the product demo and the honest offer carry the authenticity. Slang also dates fast; some of this may read as stale by the time it's live.

---

## 4. Compliance / truthful-advertising risks

- **Unsupported environmental claim (Card 5 + caption).** "sustainable by design," "ditch single-use — the planet will thank you" with *no* material, recycled-content, lifecycle, durability, or certification support. Under FTC Green Guides, unqualified environmental benefit claims need substantiation. **Either substantiate with specifics or cut the sustainability framing.**
- **False scarcity.** "before they're gone" / "tap shop now before they sell out" implies limited stock. If it isn't actually limited, that's a deceptive urgency claim. Drop it or make it true.
- **Missing paid-partnership disclosure.** The creator plan doesn't specify FTC disclosure. Every seeded creator post needs a clear, conspicuous disclosure (e.g., paid-partnership label + #ad). This is required, not optional.
- **Targeting minors** (see §2) — also a compliance issue, not just a waste one.

---

## 5. Accessibility (a stated requirement, currently unmet)

The plan requires accessibility and then provides none of it:

- **No alt text on any card** — add descriptive alt text for all five.
- **No captions/transcript for the Card 3 video** — feed video autoplays muted, so an uncaptioned demo loses much of its value even for sighted users. Add burned-in or platform captions + a transcript.
- **Color-only meaning on Card 2** — the recommended/best-value option is signaled *only* by a green ring (fails WCAG "use of color"). Add a text label or badge ("Best value / Most popular") that doesn't depend on color.
- **Card 4 contrast + density** — light-on-light text over a busy image at small mobile sizes is unreadable for many. Set contrast minimums, cap overlay text, and put dense details on the landing page instead.

---

## 6. Creator / UGC strategy

- **Selecting on follower count (250k+) + grid aesthetic only is a weak basis** for a conversion campaign. No vetting for audience fit, engagement quality, comment sentiment, or brand-values alignment means you may buy reach with little purchase intent behind it.
- **Audience-age skew is unvetted** — a large-following creator may skew heavily to minors, which collides with your no-minors constraint. Vet audience age composition explicitly.
- **Identical reused copy across six creators** undercuts the authenticity bet and can trigger user/platform backlash. Give creators the product, the offer, and the disclosure requirement, and let them speak in their own voice.

---

## What to change before launch (non-negotiable)

1. **Age → 18–29, exclude minors.**
2. **Destination → dedicated Sling landing page**, not homepage.
3. **Add guest checkout.**
4. **Make purchase the primary metric; add CAC/ROAS/contribution margin and return-rate tracking.**
5. **Add FTC paid-partnership disclosure to all creator posts.**
6. **Substantiate or remove the sustainability claim; remove false scarcity.**
7. **Add accessibility basics:** alt text, video captions/transcript, non-color signal on Card 2, fix Card 4 contrast/density.

## What to test (after the fixes)

- **Hook A/B:** demo/clarity-led (current Card 3 logic) vs. vibe-led (current Card 1).
- **Copy register:** heavy slang vs. plainer, benefit-led — measured on purchases, not saves.
- **Card order:** demo-first vs. current order.
- **Offer emphasis:** which risk-reducer moves conversion most (free returns vs. free shipping vs. 15% off) — surface the winner earlier.
- **Age bands within 18–29**, and — before committing to Instagram-only — a small test to validate the single-channel assumption rather than asserting it.

---

**Net:** keep the product demo and the honest offer; they're the real strengths. Fix the funnel (destination, checkout), the targeting, the compliance items, and the measurement so the campaign actually pursues — and can prove — first purchases. Right now it's engineered to generate views and slang, not sales, and to leave you unable to tell the difference.

---

## Company and category

**Loopwell** is a US direct-to-consumer brand that sells one accessory for
reusable water bottles: the **Loopwell Sling**. The Sling is a universal
crossbody strap with a silicone grip cradle that clips onto most standard
wide- and narrow-mouth bottles, plus a small zip pocket sized for a card, key,
or transit pass. It is an add-on for a bottle the customer already owns; the
brand does not sell bottles. Everything is sold and shipped from
loopwell-example.com.

## Geography and language

United States only. English-language creative and site.

## Target audience

Intended audience: **US Gen Z adults, explicitly ages 18–29**. These are
first-time prospects. The brand also markets the Sling as an everyday carry
accessory for commuters, students, gym-goers, and festival-goers, but the paid
campaign audience for this asset is defined as Gen Z adults 18–29.

## Customer state

Every person reached is a **new prospect**: they have never visited
loopwell-example.com, never bought anything from Loopwell, and are not on any
Loopwell list. They are cold paid-social traffic seeing the brand for the first
time in an Instagram feed.

## Business objective

**Acquire first-time purchasers.** The goal of this campaign is a completed
first purchase from a new customer, not awareness, list growth, or engagement
for its own sake.

## Customer objective (as understood by the team)

Let a first-time viewer quickly decide **whether the Sling solves a real
everyday problem for them — carrying a bottle hands-free — and whether it is
worth $34.**

## Channel, placement, and device

- **Channel:** a single paid **Instagram carousel** ad. No other channel or
  placement is used in this campaign.
- **Placement:** mobile Instagram feed.
- **Device:** phones. The asset is designed for and delivered to the in-feed
  mobile experience.

## Offer, pricing, shipping, and returns

- **Price:** the Loopwell Sling is **$34**.
- **Incentive:** **15% off the first order** for new customers (first order
  only). No larger discount is offered.
- **Shipping:** **free shipping** on every order; orders **ship within 2
  business days** from a US warehouse and typically **arrive in 3–6 business

- **Returns:** **30-day returns, no questions asked**, with a prepaid return
  label included in the box. The return policy is stated plainly on the asset.

- **Five carousel cards. One caption. One landing-page destination.**
- **No customer testimonials, named reviews, or fabricated ratings.**
- **No discount larger than 15%.**
- **No targeting or creative directed at minors.**
- **Accessibility requirements apply** to the creative and the destination.
- US regulatory context applies, including truthful-advertising expectations
  and paid-partnership disclosure for creator content (FTC).

## Conversion event

The single defined conversion event is a **completed first purchase at
loopwell-example.com**, tracked as one purchase event in analytics.

## Targeting assumptions (as written in the media plan)

- **Channel assumption:** "Nearly all Gen Z discover new products through
  Instagram, so Instagram alone is enough to reach this audience." No source,
  first-party data, or test is attached to this claim, and no other channel or
  placement is considered.
- **Audience line (as written in the media plan):** "Target **all Gen Z
  users** on Instagram — we don't want to over-narrow the audience." The current

- **Voice:** the plan directs writers to "sound native to Gen Z" by leaning

## Creator / UGC strategy (as written in the plan)

- The plan will seed the campaign with **six creators**, selected **mainly by
  follower count (250k+ followers) and whether their grid matches the brand's
  aesthetic**. There is no vetting for audience fit, engagement quality,

  skews to minors.
- Creator posts will reuse the carousel's copy and hashtags. The plan does not
  specify a paid-partnership disclosure.

## The carousel artifact

Five cards, one caption, one CTA, one destination. Draft copy is verbatim below.

### Card 1 — Hook

- **Visual:** a close-up of a bottle being slung crossbody as someone walks,

- **Headline (overlay):** "the most authentic bottle strap on your FYP fr"
- **Overlay copy:** "no cap this hits different bestie 💅 it's giving hydration,
  it's giving main character energy — you're gonna be lowkey obsessed, periodt"

### Card 2 — Options

- **Visual:** three Slings shown side by side for narrow-mouth, wide-mouth, and

- **Headline (overlay):** "pick your fit bestie"
- **Overlay copy:** "which one's giving you? ⬅️➡️"
- **Note:** the **recommended, best-value option is indicated only by a green

### Card 3 — How it works

- **Visual:** a short in-feed video loop that clearly demonstrates the product:

  hands-free, then drops a phone and a key into the zip pocket. Each step is

- **Headline (overlay):** "clips on in 2 seconds"
- **Overlay copy:** "any standard bottle. hands free. pocket for your card + key."

### Card 4 — Details

- **Visual:** a lifestyle photo of a crowded festival, with a large block of

- **Headline (overlay):** "everything you need to know"
- **Overlay copy (a dense block of text over the photo):** "universal fit for
  narrow + wide mouth bottles • adjustable strap 20–48 in • silicone grip
  cradle • zip pocket fits card key transit pass • sweatproof + rinsable •
  $34 with 15% off your first order • free shipping, ships in 2 business days,
  arrives 3–6 business days • 30-day returns no questions asked, prepaid label
  in the box • #hydration #everydaycarry #festivaltok #fyp #loopwell"

### Card 5 — Sustainability + CTA

- **Visual:** a sunrise nature shot.
- **Headline (overlay):** "sustainable by design 🌱"
- **Overlay copy:** "ditch single-use — the planet will thank you. tap to cop
  yours before they're gone."
- **Note:** no material, recycled-content, lifecycle, durability, or
  certification detail supports the sustainability line.

### Caption (one caption for the whole carousel)

> ok bestie the loopwell sling is lowkey the everyday carry hack you didn't know
> you needed 😭 no cap it hits different — clip it on any standard bottle, sling
> it crossbody, drop your card + key in the pocket, and you're OUT. it's giving
> hands-free main character energy periodt. $34, 15% off your first order, free
> shipping (ships in 2 biz days), 30-day returns no questions asked. don't be
> delulu, tap shop now before they sell out 💅 #loopwell #everydaycarry #fyp

### CTA and destination

- **CTA button:** "Shop now"
- **Destination:** the CTA links to the **Loopwell homepage
  (loopwell-example.com)**, not to a product-specific page for the Sling. A
  first-time viewer lands on the general homepage and must find the Sling
  themselves.

### Purchase path (mobile)

- On mobile, the checkout **requires creating an account (email + password)
  before a first purchase can be completed**. There is **no guest checkout**.
  A new prospect must register an account before they can buy.

## Measurement plan (as written)

- **Primary success metrics:** **impressions, reach, and video views**
  (3-second plays). These are the numbers the plan will report as success.
- **Secondary metrics:** saves and shares.
- There is **no holdout or control group**, so the campaign cannot show whether
  it drove purchases that would not have happened anyway.
- There is **no incrementality or matched-audience design**.
- There is **no contribution-margin, CAC, or return-on-ad-spend measure**, even

- There is **no repeat-purchase or 60-day retention measure**.
- There is **no refund-, return-rate-, or chargeback measure**, even though the

## Design and accessibility notes (as written in the plan)

- **Aesthetic:** unpolished, phone-shot, "native to the feed."
- **Alt text:** none is written for any card.
- **Screen-reader / captions:** the plan provides no screen-reader description

- **Meaning conveyed by color:** yes — the recommended option on Card 2 is shown
  only by a green ring (see Card 2).
- **Text density and contrast:** Card 4 sets a large block of overlay text over

  guidance on minimum text size, contrast, or how much overlay text fits legibly
  on a phone screen.

---

## Your task

Review this paid-social carousel for its intended audience and tell the team
whether it is likely to work, why, what is weak or unsupported, and what should
change or be tested.

# Generational Marketing Review

## Verdict

**Fit:** Weak fit (as currently drafted)
**Confidence:** Medium — the structural and compliance flaws below are directly observable and high-certainty; the open question is only how a corrected version would perform, which is untested.
**Recommended decision:** Do not proceed as drafted. Fix the compliance and conversion-path blockers, then revise and retest.

The underlying product, offer, and logistics are sound and the Card 3 demo is genuinely good. But the campaign as written contains several override-level problems — it targets minors despite an explicit ban, makes an unsubstantiated environmental claim, omits creator paid-partnership disclosure, fails multiple accessibility requirements, routes cold buyers to a homepage behind a forced-account checkout, and measures reach instead of the purchases it says it exists to produce. Any one of these would cap the score; together they make the current draft unshippable, even though the fixes are mostly mechanical.

## Audience-definition check

- **Cohort:** US Gen Z adults (**Provided fact**) — but the operative ad set targets **13–65+** (**Observed feature**), which contradicts the stated cohort and reaches minors and the 30–65+ range the brief excludes.
- **Birth range or life stage:** Ages **18–29**, young adults; use-cases named as commuters, students, gym-goers, festival-goers (**Provided fact**).
- **Geography:** United States only, English (**Provided fact**).
- **Category:** Add-on crossbody strap for a reusable bottle the customer already owns; brand sells no bottles (**Provided fact**).
- **Customer state:** Cold, first-time prospects — never visited, never purchased, not on any list (**Provided fact**).
- **Objective:** Acquire first-time purchasers; one completed purchase is the sole conversion event (**Provided fact**).
- **Missing context:** Source for the "nearly all Gen Z discover via Instagram" claim; any first-party audience data; the actual homepage/landing experience beyond "must find the Sling"; real inventory status behind the "before they sell out" line; any substantiation for the sustainability claim; brand voice guidance beyond "use slang."

## Executive summary

The team has a legitimately reviewable, well-specified asset with a real everyday-carry need and a low-risk offer (free shipping, 30-day no-questions returns, prepaid label). Those are strengths. The problems are not subtle audience-fit judgment calls; they are concrete defects that defeat the campaign's own stated goal. The single defined objective is a first purchase, yet the destination (homepage, not the Sling page), the checkout (forced account, no guest), and the measurement plan (impressions/reach/views, no purchase or CAC/ROAS, no holdout) are all misaligned with purchasing. On top of that sit hard compliance issues: a 13–65+ ad set against an explicit "no minors" constraint, an unsupported "sustainable by design / the planet will thank you" claim on a product that is itself a strap, missing FTC paid-partnership disclosure for six creators chosen only by follower count and aesthetic, and accessibility failures across every card. The generational strategy leans on "Gen Z is obsessed with authenticity" as settled fact and then buries product clarity under heavy slang — the opposite of what earns a cold first purchase.

## Scorecard

| Dimension | Score 0–4 | Evidence | Concern | Recommended action |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Audience definition | 1 | Stated cohort 18–29, US, cold prospects | Ad set is 13–65+ and "all Gen Z"; reaches minors and out-of-cohort ages, violating the no-minors constraint | Set the ad set to 18–29; exclude 13–17 explicitly; align creator audiences to adults |
| Customer need and context | 2 | Real hands-free carry need; Card 3 demonstrates it literally | Creative leads with "most authentic" and slang, not the need; leans on age-as-need reasoning | Lead Card 1 with the problem/benefit, not a self-label |
| Value proposition | 2 | Universal fit, hands-free, zip pocket, 2-second clip are concrete and differentiated for an accessory | Buried under slang on Card 1; proof thin for a cold $34 ask | Surface the benefit and the demo earlier; tie fit-options to the "will it fit my bottle" objection |
| Message and tone | 1 | Dense slang across headlines, overlays, caption ("no cap," "delulu," "periodt," "cop") | Forced-slang and condescension risk; self-proclaimed authenticity is self-undermining; clarity suffers | Cut slang density sharply; keep voice casual but let the product be legible |
| Creative and format | 2 | Mobile-native; strong Card 3 demo; Card 2 fit options useful | Card 4 dense text over busy photo; Card 1 hierarchy weak; Card 5 off-topic | Rebuild Card 4 as scannable spec card; promote the demo; fix Card 1 hierarchy |
| Channel and platform fit | 2 | Instagram carousel format is native to placement | "Instagram alone is enough" is uncited and untested; single-channel bet with no defined channel role | Keep IG for this test but label the single-channel assumption and plan a channel test |
| Trust and proof | 1 | Card 3 demo is credible; returns/shipping stated plainly | No testimonials (constraint); unsupported sustainability + scarcity claims erode trust; no creator disclosure | Replace/support unproven claims with demonstrable specs; add disclosure |
| Offer and purchase friction | 1 | Price, 15% off, free shipping, returns all stated clearly | CTA lands on homepage not the Sling page; forced account creation, no guest checkout — for cold buyers | Deep-link to the Sling PDP; enable guest checkout |
| Customer experience and fulfillment | 2 | Ship-in-2-days, 3–6-day arrival, 30-day no-questions returns, prepaid label — genuinely reassuring | Forced-account onboarding; homepage landing; no retention/return-rate tracking | Keep the strong policy language; remove onboarding friction; track returns |
| Inclusion, accessibility, privacy, ethics | 0 | No alt text; no captions/transcript for Card 3 video; meaning by color only (green ring); dense light-on-light Card 4; minors targeted; unsubstantiated green claim; "before they sell out" pressure | Multiple accessibility failures where requirements explicitly apply; likely FTC exposure on green claim and disclosure | Treat as launch blocker (see Critical fixes) |
| Measurement and experimentation | 0 | Primary metrics: impressions, reach, 3-sec views; no holdout, no incrementality, no CAC/ROAS/margin, no return or retention measure | Cannot show whether the campaign produced the purchases that are its only objective | Make purchases/CAC/ROAS primary; add a holdout or geo test; track returns and repeat |
| Evidence quality | 1 | Offer/logistics facts are concrete and clear | Channel, authenticity, and sustainability claims are uncited and presented as fact; no first-party data; assumptions unlabeled | Label assumptions; source or drop behavioral claims; substantiate or cut green claim |

**Critical override applied:** the accessibility, targeting-of-minors, unsubstantiated-environmental-claim, and missing-disclosure problems each independently cap the overall verdict regardless of the stronger dimensions.

## What works

- **Card 3 is the campaign's best asset.** A literal, in-order, ~3-second demonstration (clip on → sling crossbody → drop phone/key in pocket) is exactly the proof a cold prospect needs for a mechanical accessory. It should be more central, not card three.
- **The offer terms are stated plainly and de-risk the purchase:** $34, 15% off first order, free shipping, ship-in-2-days, 3–6-day arrival, 30-day no-questions returns with a prepaid label. For a first-time $34 buy, no-questions returns plus a prepaid label is a real objection-remover.
- **Card 2 addresses the single biggest fit objection for a "universal" accessory** — will it fit my bottle — by showing narrow-mouth, wide-mouth, and sport options.
- **Format matches placement.** A mobile, in-feed, phone-shot carousel is appropriate for IG feed on phones.

## What may fail

- **The conversion path defeats the objective.** "Shop now" → homepage means a cold viewer must self-navigate to the Sling; then checkout forces account creation before a first purchase. Each step is a documented drop-off point, stacked directly on the one action the campaign is paid to produce.
- **The audience is wrong.** A 13–65+ ad set against a "no minors" constraint is both a compliance violation and a spend leak; much of the delivery will fall outside 18–29.
- **The measurement plan cannot detect success or failure.** Reporting impressions/reach/views for a purchase objective, with no holdout and no CAC/ROAS/margin, means the team could "hit" every reported metric while losing money on every $34 order carrying 15% off and free two-way shipping.
- **The voice buries the value.** Stacked slang ("no cap," "it's giving," "periodt," "delulu," "cop") plus a self-proclaimed "most authentic" label reads as performing an assumed identity rather than helping someone decide. For cold traffic, clarity converts; costume does not.
- **Trust leaks.** An unsupported sustainability claim, a scarcity line ("before they sell out") with no stated basis, and six undisclosed paid creators are the kinds of signals that generate negative comments — the exact social proof a cold audience reads before buying.

## Stereotype, evidence, and freshness flags

- **Stereotype — "Gen Z is obsessed with authenticity" as settled fact.** Treated as a proven trait and made the central creative bet. This is a generalization, not evidence. Worse, the execution announces its own authenticity ("the most authentic bottle strap on your FYP"), which is self-contradicting; authenticity is demonstrated, not claimed. **Convert to hypothesis and test** benefit-led vs identity-led framing.
- **Stereotype — "sound native to Gen Z" via heavy slang.** Equating a cohort with a slang register risks condescension and forced-slang failure, and it degrades legibility for cold buyers. Not evidence of what this audience responds to.
- **Evidence — "Nearly all Gen Z discover new products through Instagram, so Instagram alone is enough."** Uncited platform-behavior claim presented as fact, with no source, date, geography, sample, or first-party data, driving a single-channel bet with no test. **Label as Assumption; do not present as fact.**
- **Evidence — unsubstantiated environmental claim.** "Sustainable by design," "ditch single-use — the planet will thank you," with no material, recycled-content, lifecycle, durability, or certification support — and the product is a strap for a bottle the customer already owns, so the "ditch single-use" logic isn't even connected to the item. This is a truthful-advertising/FTC green-claims exposure, not just a weak line.
- **Evidence — unsupported scarcity.** "before they're gone" / "before they sell out" with no stated inventory basis risks deceptive urgency.
- **Freshness/currency — no dated, sourced behavioral data anywhere.** All audience/channel reasoning rests on undated generalizations. The concrete, current facts in the asset are the offer and logistics, which are fine.

## Priority fixes

### Critical (launch blockers — fix before any spend)

1. **Restrict targeting to adults 18–29.** Change the ad set from 13–65+ to 18–29 and add an explicit under-18 exclusion. Screen creators so their audiences skew adult; drop any that skew to minors.
2. **Add FTC paid-partnership disclosure** to every creator post (clear, conspicuous, in-post), and put it in the creator brief. Do not launch creator content without it.
3. **Substantiate or remove the sustainability claim.** Either provide specific, verifiable support (material, recycled content, certification, lifecycle) or cut Card 5's environmental copy. Do not run the claim as-is.
4. **Fix accessibility across all cards:** write alt text for every still; add captions and a transcript for the Card 3 video; add a non-color label/badge/text to mark the recommended option on Card 2 (color must not be the only signal); rebuild Card 4 for minimum text size, sufficient contrast, and no light-on-light overlay.
5. **Point the CTA to the Sling product page,** not the homepage.
6. **Enable guest checkout** so a first purchase does not require account creation.

### High

7. **Realign measurement to the objective:** make completed purchases, CAC, and ROAS/contribution margin the primary metrics; add a holdout or geo-based test for incrementality; track return/refund rate and at least a 60-day repeat measure. Keep impressions/reach/views as diagnostics only.
8. **Rewrite Card 1** to lead with the problem/benefit (hands-free bottle carry) and show the product in use, not a self-labeled "most authentic" claim.
9. **Cut slang density** across headlines, overlays, and caption; keep a casual voice but let the offer and demo read cleanly. Remove the scarcity pressure lines unless inventory truly justifies them.
10. **Add a defined role for the single-channel choice** and label it an assumption; plan at least one channel/placement test rather than asserting "Instagram alone is enough."

### Medium

11. **Promote the Card 3 demo earlier** in the sequence and make the fit-guidance on Card 2 explicit (which option for which bottle).
12. **Turn Card 4 into a scannable spec card** (short lines, off-image or high-contrast panel) rather than a dense block over a festival photo.
13. **Vet creators on engagement quality, comment sentiment, and brand-values fit,** not follower count and grid aesthetic alone.

## Test plan

| Hypothesis | Variant | Primary metric | Guardrail | Decision rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Restricting to 18–29 (vs 13–65+) improves efficiency and removes minors | A: 18–29 only, under-18 excluded; B: current 13–65+ | CAC (cost per completed purchase) | Zero impressions served to under-18 (compliance, non-negotiable) | Adopt A if CAC ≤ B; adopt A regardless on compliance grounds |
| Deep-linking to the Sling PDP (vs homepage) raises purchase rate | A: CTA → Sling PDP; B: CTA → homepage | Purchase conversion rate per click | PDP mobile load time within target | Adopt A if CVR uplift is positive and stable over the test window |
| Guest checkout (vs forced account) lifts completed first purchases | A: guest checkout enabled; B: forced account | Checkout completion rate | Chargeback/fraud rate not materially higher | Adopt A if completion rises without a fraud increase |
| Benefit-led Card 1 (vs "most authentic" slang hook) converts cold traffic better | A: problem/hands-free hook; B: current hook | Click-through → completed purchase | Negative-comment / hide rate | Adopt the higher-purchase variant if comment sentiment is not worse |
| Reduced-slang, high-clarity copy (vs heavy slang) converts better | A: plain-clear voice; B: heavy slang | Purchase CVR | Negative-comment rate | Adopt A if CVR ≥ B and sentiment equal or better |
| A proof/spec Card 5 (vs sustainability slot) supports purchase | A: demo/spec proof card; B: substantiated sustainability card (only if substantiation exists) | Purchase CVR | No unsupported claims present in either variant | Adopt the higher-CVR compliant variant; do not test an unsubstantiated claim |

Note: the sustainability line is a substantiate-or-remove item, not an A/B question — do not test a claim that may be deceptive. Treat true inventory scarcity the same way.

## Evidence register

- **Provided facts:** US-only, English; audience defined as Gen Z adults 18–29; cold first-time prospects; objective is a completed first purchase; single IG carousel, mobile feed; $34, 15% off first order, free shipping, ship in 2 business days, arrive 3–6, 30-day no-questions returns with prepaid label; five cards, one caption, one CTA, one destination; constraints include no minors, no larger discount, no fabricated reviews, accessibility applies, FTC truthful-advertising and paid-partnership disclosure apply.
- **Observed features:** ad set set to 13–65+; CTA links to homepage, not the Sling PDP; mobile checkout forces account creation, no guest checkout; primary metrics are impressions/reach/views with no holdout, CAC, ROAS, return, or retention measure; no alt text, no captions/transcript; Card 2 recommendation shown only by a green ring; Card 4 dense/low-contrast overlay; Card 5 environmental claim with no support; scarcity language in Card 5 and caption; six creators chosen by follower count and aesthetic with no disclosure specified.
- **Inferences:** the homepage destination plus forced account plus reach-based metrics will systematically suppress and obscure the purchases the campaign exists to drive; heavy slang plus self-proclaimed authenticity reduces legibility for a cold audience.
- **Assumptions (labeled, unverified):** "Instagram alone is enough" to reach the audience; "Gen Z is obsessed with authenticity" as a purchasing driver; that inventory is genuinely limited enough to justify "before they sell out."
